# Neural Basis Functions

Also called: Fourier basis, General basis form, b basis

## Overview
Neural Basis Functions are a set of parameterized mathematical functions used to represent the directional component $\tilde{H}$ in the rendering equation, allowing for the ablation and comparison of different functional forms for view-dependent color prediction [S1]. They solve the problem of encoding viewing direction into a differentiable feature vector that a neural network can process. What sets them apart from siblings like [Spherical Harmonics Encoder](4390-spherical-harmonics-encoder.md) is the explicit use of custom analytic forms (Fourier, Ka,b, Pa,b) tailored to specific viewing constraints (e.g., forward-facing hemispheres) rather than relying on standard orthogonal polynomial bases [S1].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism involves mapping a viewing direction vector $v$ to a fixed-length feature vector $\tilde{H}(v)$. For forward-facing scenarios, the viewing angle $v$ is constrained to a hemisphere. In this case, the $z$-component $v_z$ is fully determined by the $x$ and $y$ components via the constraint:
$$ v_z = \sqrt{1 - v_x^2 - v_y^2} $$
Consequently, the basis functions can be parameterized using only $v_x$ and $v_y$ [S1]. The general form of the neural basis combines real and imaginary parts of complex-valued functions $K_{a,b}$ and $P_{a,b}$ [S1].

## Subtopics

### Fourier Basis ($\tilde{H}_{FS}$)
A basis similar to the positional encoding used in NeRF [22]. It is defined for forward-facing scenarios using only $v_x$ and $v_y$. It is chosen when a simple, high-frequency periodic encoding is sufficient and the viewing domain is hemispherical. See [Fourier Basis](#fourier-basis).

### Ka,b and Pa,b Basis
A general analytic form using parameters $a, b, m$. It is chosen for more complex view-dependent effects where the Fourier basis may be insufficient. It is defined for general viewing directions. See [Ka,b and Pa,b Basis](#kab-and-pab-basis).

## Background
The concept was introduced in "NeX: Real-time View Synthesis with Neural Basis Expansion" (CVPR 2021) by Ben Mildenhall, Pratul P. Srinivasan, Rodrigo Ortiz-Cayon, Nima Khademi Kalantari, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Ren Ng, and Abhishek Kar [S1]. The work builds upon the neural radiance field (NeRF) framework [22] and aims to provide practical view synthesis with prescriptive sampling guidelines. The ablation study of these basis functions is detailed in the supplementary material of the NeX paper [S1].

## Fourier Basis
The Fourier basis $\tilde{H}_{FS}(v)$ is designed for forward-facing scenarios where the viewing angle covers a hemisphere. It uses the positional encoding approach similar to NeRF [22]. Given the viewing angle components $v_x$ and $v_y$, and a maximum frequency index $N$, the basis is computed as:
$$ \tilde{H}_{FS}(v) = [\cos(2^{-1}\pi v_x), \sin(2^{-1}\pi v_x), \dots, \cos(2^N \pi v_x), \sin(2^N \pi v_x), \dots, \cos(2^N \pi v_y), \sin(2^N \pi v_y)] $$
Note: The source text lists the sequence as ending with $v_y$ terms, implying interleaved or concatenated frequencies for both axes. The exact ordering in the source is: $\cos(2^{-1}\pi v_x), \sin(2^{-1}\pi v_x), \dots, \cos(2^N \pi v_y), \sin(2^N \pi v_y)$ [S1].

## Ka,b and Pa,b Basis
This general form uses complex-valued functions $K_{a,b}(v)$ and $P_{a,b}(v)$ defined by parameters $a, b, m$. The components $v_x, v_y, v_z$ are the viewing angle components.

The function $K_{a,b}(v)$ is defined as:
$$ K_{a,b}(v) = \left( \frac{v_x}{\sqrt{v_z - a}} \frac{v_z - a}{v_z + 1} \right)^m \left( \frac{v_y}{\sqrt{v_z + 1}} \frac{v_z - a}{v_z + 1} \right)^m $$
The function $P_{a,b}(v)$ is defined as:
$$ P_{a,b}(v) = v_z^{1-a} \frac{v_z - 1 + m + 1}{b + 2m + 2} $$
The final neural basis $\tilde{H}(v)$ combines the real and imaginary parts of these functions:
$$ \tilde{H}(v) = [ \text{Re}(K_{a,b}(v)), \text{Im}(K_{a,b}(v)), \text{Re}(P_{a,b}(v) \cdot K_{a,b}(v)), \text{Re}(K_{a,b}(v)), \text{Re}(K_{a,b}(v)) ] $$
Note: The source lists $\text{Re}(K_{a,b}(v))$ twice at the end of the vector [S1]. The parameters $a, b, m$ are not explicitly defined in the provided notes, but are treated as configurable hyperparameters [S1].
